How Often Should You Drain a Pool in Arizona?

In the desert, pool water does not wear out on a calendar. It wears out as evaporation leaves minerals behind. Here is how to tell when it is time, how much to drain, and where each Valley city lets the water go.

Call (623) 240-0428 Jump to the city rules table
  1. Home
  2. Draining a Pool in Arizona

How often should I drain my pool in Arizona? It is one of the most common questions Valley pool owners ask, and the honest answer is: less often than you might think, and only when the water tells you. A desert pool loses water to the sky every day and keeps everything that was dissolved in it. Over a few summers that build-up makes the water hard to balance, and that, not a date on the calendar, is what decides when fresh water makes sense.

Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro is a free phone line, not a pool company. How often should I drain my pool in Arizona? What the sources say

No agency sets a draining schedule for backyard pools, and the official guidance leans toward draining rarely. The Arizona Department of Water Resources (ADWR) says swimming pools seldom need draining. Scottsdale's water conservation guidance agrees, saying pools seldom require draining when chemical levels are properly maintained. The City of Mesa recommends asking a pool professional when draining is needed and how often.

The clearest test comes from the pool industry. The Pool and Hot Tub Alliance (PHTA), the pool and spa industry's trade association, recommends that total dissolved solids, or TDS, stay no more than 1,500 parts per million above the level measured when the pool was first filled. TDS is simply everything dissolved in the water: calcium, salts, stabilizer, and leftovers from every chemical ever added. PHTA says going past that line may mean the water needs a partial or complete drain, as long as drought rules or other limits on draining are not in effect.

Salt pools work on a different baseline. A salt chlorine generator needs salt in the water, often around 3,000 parts per million, so a salt pool's TDS starts high. Pool and Spa News suggests diluting a salt pool when TDS runs 1,500 above the fill water plus that salt, which for a typical system means somewhere around 4,500.

The practical answer. Have calcium hardness, stabilizer (cyanuric acid) and TDS tested a few times a year, and write the numbers down. When they climb past what the pool company can balance with chemicals, plan a partial drain. How long that takes depends on your fill water, how much evaporates and how much chemical goes in, which is why testing beats the calendar.

Why Arizona pool water wears out

ADWR says a standard uncovered pool in Arizona loses four to six feet of water a year to evaporation, most of it in summer. When water evaporates, the minerals in it stay in the pool. The top off water then brings in more. ADWR adds that, counting refills and backwashing, an uncovered pool uses roughly its own volume of water each year, and that draining the pool doubles that amount.

The fill water starts hard. The City of Phoenix's 2025 water quality report lists total hardness of 172 to 302 parts per million, about 10 to 17.6 grains per gallon, and total dissolved solids of 464 to 716 parts per million. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's non-enforceable taste and appearance guideline for TDS in drinking water is 500 milligrams per liter, so Valley tap water starts near or above it before a single inch evaporates.

Three things build up as a result. Calcium hardness climbs, and in hot water calcium comes out as white scale on tile, in heaters and on salt cell plates. Cyanuric acid, the stabilizer that shields chlorine from ultraviolet light, builds up from stabilized chlorine tablets and only leaves when water leaves. And general TDS rises with every bag of salt, every dose of chlorine and every inch of top off water. A careful pool technician uses the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI), a calculation that combines pH, alkalinity, calcium and temperature, to judge whether the water will deposit scale or eat at plaster. When the numbers make that balance impossible to hold, dilution is the fix.

Signs it may be time for fresh water

None of these alone proves a drain is needed. Each one is a reason to have the water tested properly and the numbers compared with your fill water.

Signs that pool water may need partial replacement, what they suggest and what to test
What you noticeWhat it can meanWhat to have tested
White crust returns on the tile soon after a tile cleaningCalcium hardness is so high the water keeps dropping scaleCalcium hardness, pH, alkalinity, the LSI at summer water temperature
Chlorine reads fine but the water clouds or grows algae anywayStabilizer may be high enough to slow chlorine downCyanuric acid and free chlorine together
Chemicals seem to stop working or the water tastes saltyTotal dissolved solids may be far above the fill levelTDS, compared with a tap water sample (and the salt level on a salt pool)
Scale on the salt cell or heater, or a filter that clogs with fine crustMineral build-up in equipmentCalcium hardness and LSI; have the equipment looked at
Years of topping off with no water replacedEverything dissolved has been concentrating the whole timeA full panel: calcium, stabilizer and TDS

A home test kit is fine for chlorine and pH. Calcium, stabilizer and TDS are worth having tested by a pool company, since the decision to drain rests on them. The pool tile cleaning page explains what happens to scale that has already formed, and weekly pool cleaning and maintenance covers the routine testing that spots the trend early.

Partial drain or full drain?

Most of the time the goal is to lower the numbers, not to see the bottom. How far to go depends on how high the readings are and whether any work needs the pool empty.

Partial drain and refill

The water is lowered part of the way and topped back up with fresh tap water, which dilutes calcium, stabilizer and TDS by roughly the share replaced. The finish stays mostly underwater, less water is used, and the pool is back in service sooner. If one round is not enough, a second can follow once the water is retested.

Full drain

An empty pool is needed for resurfacing, many structural repairs and some acid work, which is a job for a professional. It also carries more risk. The National Plaster Council warns that where groundwater is high, an empty pool can be pushed up out of the ground, and advises confirming a hydrostatic relief valve is in place before draining.

Why the season matters

The National Plaster Council recommends keeping a plaster finish submerged for its durability and notes that fresh plaster still curing can be harmed when water is removed. National Weather Service normals for Phoenix show average highs above 100 degrees from June through August. Ask the company how it will protect an exposed finish in that sun, and whether a cooler month would suit.

Watch the winter sewer bill

Some cities base the sewer charge on winter water use. Mesa notes that filling a pool from December through March can affect your sewer fee, while filling from April through November does not. Scottsdale also averages winter water use for sewer billing. Check your own city before you set the date.

Where drained and backwashed pool water may go, city by city

Every Valley city keeps pool water out of the storm drain system, because storm drains carry water untreated to washes, retention basins and rivers. Pool water carries chlorine, salt and dirt. The details differ, though, and they apply to filter backwash as well as a full drain. These are the rules each city publishes; check the linked page for yours before any water leaves the yard.

Valley city rules on where drained or backwashed pool water may go
CityAllowedNot allowed, and other limits
PhoenixThe sanitary sewer cleanout on your property, recommended at no more than 12 gallons per minute, or watering your own landscaping.No storm drain (City Code Chapter 32C), street, alley or right of way. Homes with no cleanout may discharge dechlorinated water to the right of way only by permit, under 50 gallons per minute and under 1 part per million chlorine; backwash and saltwater are excluded.
ScottsdaleYour own landscape after letting chlorine dissipate for 3 to 7 days, or the sewer cleanout at no more than 50 gallons per minute.Never to the street, where storm drains feed the flood control system and the Salt River.
MesaThe sanitary sewer cleanout on your property, with no notification or permit, at about 12 gallons per minute and near neutral pH (6 to 8).Streets, gutters and storm drains are discouraged and may violate city code. No permanent drain line from the pool to the sewer.
ChandlerKeep the water on your own property, or send it to the sewer cleanout on your property; no permit needed. Backwash may go onto your own landscaping. About 12 gallons per minute is suggested.A pipe or hose to the street, an alley or other right of way counts as a connection to the storm drain system and is prohibited.
GilbertYour yard first, if it can absorb the water without runoff; the sewer cleanout for the rest, and for salt pools or water high in chemicals. No permit required.No backwash or filter water into the street or gutter, no permanent pipe to the cleanout or curb, and the cleanout route is not for lake communities. Follow your HOA policy too.

Contact the city's Environmental Services before draining a residential pool over 35,000 gallons.
GlendaleThe home's sewer cleanout for large amounts, at no more than 12 gallons per minute; backwash may irrigate landscaping.No pool or spa water into any public street, alley or right of way. Avoid salt-sensitive plants such as citrus and hibiscus.

Residential drain permits are no longer required.No pool water into the storm drain or street; backwash must stay on your property, and never onto adjacent property, easements or watercourses.
SurpriseLet it soak into your own yard without runoff, or send it to the sewer cleanout on your property.Nothing off the lot: not the street, curb, sidewalk, a retention basin or a neighbor's yard, and that includes backwash.

Using a sewer cleanout safely

A cleanout is usually a threaded cap, often black and 3 to 4 inches across, near the house. Glendale and Peoria both warn that most pool filter pumps push water out too fast for a home sewer line, which can back water up into the yard or the house, and suggest a small submersible pump instead. If there are two cleanouts, use the one closest to the house, and check showers and tubs right after the water starts flowing. Stop at once if anything backs up. Scottsdale notes that homes older than about 20 years may not have a cleanout at all. In Gilbert, grey water running into a neighbor's yard goes to Maricopa County Environmental Services at 602-506-6616.

Reverse osmosis: cleaning the water instead of dumping it

There is a middle path between living with hard water and draining it. Mobile pool water recycling uses reverse osmosis, the same process as an under-sink drinking water filter, on a much larger scale. A trailer-mounted unit is parked near the pool, hoses draw water from the deep end, the water is pushed through fine membranes that hold back dissolved minerals, and the cleaner water flows back into the pool. Pool and Spa News describes these mobile units removing cyanuric acid, total dissolved solids and calcium, among other things, while the pool stays full.

Scottsdale's water conservation guidance points to water restoration systems as a way to avoid draining, and the regional Water Use It Wisely campaign describes mobile filtration as an alternative to a drain and refill. Two cautions. First, the process is not waterless: some water is lost along the way, so ask how much and where that water goes, because your city's discharge rules still apply to it. Second, ask what the treated water will test at for calcium and TDS, so you can compare that with a partial drain.

Arizona's water picture and your pool

Much of the Valley's water comes from the Colorado River through the Central Arizona Project (CAP). The CAP reports that the river is in a Tier 1 shortage for 2026, which cuts Arizona's Colorado River supply by 512,000 acre-feet, about 30 percent of CAP's normal supply. Every full drain and refill uses a pool's worth of treated drinking water, and ADWR's model water waste ordinance lists the periodic draining of pools among the uses communities may choose to regulate.

The biggest lever is evaporation. ADWR says a pool cover can save 90 to 95 percent of the water a pool loses to evaporation, and suggests a reflective cover in the desert since covers also hold heat. Less evaporation means fewer top offs, which means fewer new minerals and a longer stretch before the water needs replacing. Using a cartridge filter, or backwashing only when the pressure gauge calls for it, saves water too. The guide to how often to clean a pool filter covers the pressure rule. One more benefit of the sewer route: Scottsdale notes that pool water sent down the sewer is treated and recycled for future use.

Safety during a drain

  • Children. A partly empty pool is still a drowning risk, and an empty one is a fall risk. Keep gates latched and never leave a child alone near the pool.
  • Chemicals. Never mix pool chemicals with each other. Store them apart, dry, shaded and out of children's reach, follow the label, and leave acid work to a professional.
  • Equipment. Do not run the pool pump dry. Ask the company how it will handle the equipment while the water is low.
  • Electricity. Keep cords and submersible pumps out of the way of standing water, and if a breaker or GFCI trips more than once, leave it off and call a professional.
  • Neighbors. Watch the hose and the yard so water does not run onto the next lot or into the street.

Questions to ask before a pool company drains your pool

  • What do calcium, stabilizer and TDS test at now, compared with my tap water?
  • Would a partial drain do it, and how much water would you replace?
  • Where will the water go, and does that match my city's rules?
  • Does my pool have a hydrostatic relief valve, and how will you protect the finish if it is exposed?
  • Would reverse osmosis treatment be a better fit, and how much water would that use?
  • If resurfacing or repair is part of the job, what is your ROC license number?

Check the license first. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) licenses contractors, and its residential classifications include R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair. Routine cleaning and water care are generally not treated as contracting work, but repairs, equipment replacement and resurfacing generally call for a licensed contractor. Ask the company for its ROC license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search (opens in a new tab) before work begins. The line does not check this for you.

Common questions

How often should I drain my pool in Arizona?

There is no fixed schedule. The Arizona Department of Water Resources says swimming pools seldom need draining, and Scottsdale's conservation guidance says the same when chemical levels are kept in range. The usual trigger is a test result: the Pool and Hot Tub Alliance recommends that total dissolved solids stay within 1,500 parts per million of the level when the pool was filled. Above that, a partial or full drain is the common fix.

How often should you change pool water in Arizona?

Change it when testing says so, not by the calendar. Water leaves a desert pool through evaporation, but calcium, salts and stabilizer stay behind, so the water gets harder to balance each summer. When calcium, stabilizer or total dissolved solids climb too high to manage, replacing part of the water is the reset. A pool company can test and tell you how much.

How often should I change the water in a spa in Arizona?

More often than a pool, because a spa holds far less water for the number of people using it. The Arizona Department of Water Resources suggests draining a spa no more than once every three to six months. Follow your spa maker's guidance and your city's rules on where the water goes.

Can I drain my pool into the street in Phoenix?

No. Under Phoenix City Code Chapter 32C, pool water may not go to the storm drain, and the city asks residents not to drain into the street, an alley or other city right of way. Use the sanitary sewer cleanout on your property, at no more than the recommended 12 gallons per minute, or water your own landscaping. Homes with no cleanout need a city permit for a right of way discharge, and backwash and saltwater are not allowed that way.

Should I drain my pool in the summer?

It is worth avoiding a full drain in peak heat if you can. The National Plaster Council recommends keeping a plaster finish submerged, and Phoenix's normal highs top 100 degrees from June through August, so an empty shell sits in hard sun. Ask the pool company how it will protect the surface if a summer drain cannot wait, and whether a cooler month works.

Is reverse osmosis a good alternative to draining a pool?

It can be. Mobile reverse osmosis units pump pool water through fine membranes on site and return cleaner water to the pool, removing much of the calcium, total dissolved solids and stabilizer without emptying it. Some water is still lost in the process, so ask the company how much and where that water goes, since city discharge rules still apply.
